newsitem.title: POLAND: POLISH NOMINAL RATES SEEN STEADY - ANALYSTS.
newsitem.headline: POLISH NOMINAL RATES SEEN STEADY - ANALYSTS.

text.p: Polish nominal interest rates are likely to stay unchanged in the near-term even if inflation dips in September because a cut would further stimulate already rapidly growing credit action, analysts said on Friday.

On Thursday the central bank said it would either keep nominal rates flat or lower them, but at a slower pace than inflation. It had ruled out the possibility of a nominal interest rate rise in the foreseeable future.
"I don't see any room for a (nominal) interest rate cut because the official rates are already low," said Andrzej Ladko, chief dealer at Bank Handlowy SA.
Earlier analysts have expected the central bank may cut rates if year-on-year inflation in September falls significantly below 20 percent.

However, some analysts said the National Bank of Poland (NBP) may raise its obligatory reserve requirements to slow the growth of credit action, which increased 2.8 percent in the first 20 days of September after a four percent jump in August.

"(Nominal) interest rates will likely remain unchanged...if inflation falls, but the NBP may use other instruments, such as reserve requirements, to curb lending to the non-financial sector," said Wlodzimierz Osak, chief dealer at Pekao SA.
Osak did not rule out a symbolic cut of interest rates if inflation pressure did not pick up in comming months, but other analysts said price growth impulses may strengthen in the comming months.

Both the central bank and the finance ministry had said year-on-year inflation should fall to around 19 percent in September from 20.5 percent in August, but analysts remained cautious about further reductions in the year-on-year index.

Many expected price growth pressure to pick up in October and the following months after this month's five percent utility price rise and uncertainty over gasoline price increases once Poland frees its fuel prices.
On Thursday, the NBP said it wanted official interest rates to rise in real terms to combat excessive growth of credit, which it said could overheat domestic demand and fuel imports.
"Such fast credit growth...is a signal of strong internal demand, which has to be cooled down," deputy central bank president Witold Kozinski told reporters on Thursday.
